content.study:
Topic at a Glance
Article 72 of the Constitution of India is titled “Power of President to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases”. It forms an integral component of The Union (Articles 52–151), located within the “Union Executive” cluster. Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023.

Constitutional Text & Anatomy
(1) The President shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence—

(a) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is by a Court Martial; further subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 10. .

(b) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends;

(c) in all cases where the sentence is a sentence of death.

(2) Nothing in sub-clause ( a) of clause (1) shall affect the power conferred by law on any officer of the Armed Forces of the Union to suspend, remit or commute a sentence passed by a Court Martial.

(3) Nothing in sub-clause ( c) of clause (1) shall affect the power to suspend, remit or commute a sentence of death exercisable by the Governor1 [omitted of a State under any law for the time being in force.

Constituent Assembly Intent & Doctrinal Foundation
The framers envisioned Article 72 as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. It regulates executive, legislative, or fundamental citizen interests to maintain the rule of law and constitutional supremacy.

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors (Senior Counsel Checklist)
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing & Remedial Path: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.
4. Evidentiary Standards: Where disputed facts or legislative arbitrariness are alleged, evidentiary burdens under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA ss. 104–106) and official gazette notifications govern the record.

Key Statutory Ingredients to Establish
1. (1) The President shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence—
2. (a) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is by a Court Martial; further subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 10. .
3. (b) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends;
4. (c) in all cases where the sentence is a sentence of death.
5. (2) Nothing in sub-clause ( a) of clause (1) shall affect the power conferred by law on any officer of the Armed Forces of the Union to suspend, remit or commute a sentence passed by a Court Martial.
6. (3) Nothing in sub-clause ( c) of clause (1) shall affect the power to suspend, remit or commute a sentence of death exercisable by the Governor1 [omitted of a State under any law for the time being in force.

Judicial Interpretation & Binding Ratios
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.

Current-Law Position & Milestone
Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. Any attempt by subordinate legislation or executive notifications to abridge the mandate of Article 72 is subject to judicial review under Articles 226 and 32.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Case Brief & Legal Assessment: Scope and Application of Article 72 (Power of President to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
Whether the State action, statutory enactment, or individual claim conforms to the constitutional mandate, procedural prerequisites, and substantive protections enshrined in Article 72 (Power of President to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases) of the Constitution of India.

II. RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
Article 72 is situated in The Union (Articles 52–151), governing the “Union Executive” dimension of Indian constitutional law.
The essential constitutional ingredients are:
1. (1) The President shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence—
2. (a) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is by a Court Martial; further subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 10. .
3. (b) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends;
4. (c) in all cases where the sentence is a sentence of death.
5. (2) Nothing in sub-clause ( a) of clause (1) shall affect the power conferred by law on any officer of the Armed Forces of the Union to suspend, remit or commute a sentence passed by a Court Martial.
6. (3) Nothing in sub-clause ( c) of clause (1) shall affect the power to suspend, remit or commute a sentence of death exercisable by the Governor1 [omitted of a State under any law for the time being in force.

III. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & REMEDIAL FORUM
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.

IV. JUDICIAL INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Supreme Court established that The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
Furthermore, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court reaffirmed that constitutional guarantees are justiciable and binding upon all state functionaries.

V. APPLICATION TO FACT PATTERNS
To apply Article 72:
1. Verify whether the impugned measure falls within the scope of the article's textual command.
2. Check whether any express exceptions, provisos, or constitutional limitations apply.
3. Subject the measure to tests of proportionality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. If an ingredient is missing or breached, the measure is unconstitutional.

VI. CONCLUSION
Article 72 stands as a vital constitutional checkpoint. Any state action in breach thereof is void and amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & CONSTITUTIONAL PHILOSOPHY
Article 72 of the Constitution of India, titled “Power of President to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases”, represents a critical cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. Situated within The Union (Articles 52–151), the provision balances state power with individual liberties and institutional accountability. The Constituent Assembly intended this provision to be an active, living guarantee rather than an ornamental declaration.
II. STATUTORY & DOCTRINAL DECONSTRUCTION
A forensic analysis of Article 72 reveals the following distinct constitutional limbs:
(a) Limb 1: (1) The President shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence—
(a) Limb 2: (a) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is by a Court Martial; further subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 10. .
(a) Limb 3: (b) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends;
(a) Limb 4: (c) in all cases where the sentence is a sentence of death.
(a) Limb 5: (2) Nothing in sub-clause ( a) of clause (1) shall affect the power conferred by law on any officer of the Armed Forces of the Union to suspend, remit or commute a sentence passed by a Court Martial.
(a) Limb 6: (3) Nothing in sub-clause ( c) of clause (1) shall affect the power to suspend, remit or commute a sentence of death exercisable by the Governor1 [omitted of a State under any law for the time being in force.
The Article must be read in conjunction with the foundational architecture of the Constitution:
1. Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: No branch of government possesses untrammelled discretion.
2. Rule of Law & Non-Arbitrariness: Every exercise of authority under Article 72 must satisfy the basic standard of fairness and reasonableness.
3. Transformative Constitutionalism: The provision must be interpreted progressively to advance justice, liberty, and equality as pledged in the Preamble.
III. JURISPRUDENTIAL EVOLUTION & LEADING CASE LAW
The Supreme Court of India has deconstructed Article 72 across several seminal judgments:
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225:
   Ratio Decidendi: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   Ratio Decidendi: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.
IV. PROCEDURAL ROADMAP & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
When approaching the Court under or in respect of Article 72:
1. Forum Selection: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Pleading Essentials: The writ petition or plaint must specifically plead:
   (a) The exact constitutional authority or violation under Article 72;
   (b) The factual narrative establishing how each statutory ingredient is satisfied or infringed;
   (c) The absence of an effective alternative remedy, or justification under the Whirlpool Corporation exceptions (breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, or complete lack of jurisdiction).
3. Evidentiary Standard: Discharge of burden under BSA ss. 104–106 and production of certified records.
V. IRAC PROBLEM ANALYSIS (PRACTICE HYPOTHETICAL)
Fact Matrix: The State issues a notification encroaching upon the domain of Article 72 without satisfying statutory preconditions.
Issue: Does the executive notification violate the constitutional guarantees and procedures of Article 72?
Rule: Under Article 72, state action is strictly conditioned by constitutional provisions and cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
Application: The impugned notification fails because it circumvents the procedural safeguards and lacks rational nexus to the constitutional objective. Applying the proportionality test, the State has failed to adopt the least intrusive means.
Conclusion: The notification is unconstitutional and void ab initio. The appropriate writ of certiorari or mandamus shall issue.
VI. CRITICAL APPRAISAL & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
Article 72 remains a vibrant instrument of governance, current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. A robust democracy requires rigorous adherence to its letter and spirit to protect the citizen against executive overreach and legislative excesses.

enhancement.definition: Article 72 of the Constitution of India empowers the President to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence in all cases where punishment is by a Court-martial, where the offence is against a Union law, and in all cases where the sentence is a sentence of death.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The clemency power is an executive constitutional prerogative, not a matter of grace or judicial power. It is exercised on the mandatory aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74) to correct possible judicial errors, temper the rigors of criminal justice with mercy, and advance the public interest, subject to limited judicial review against arbitrariness.

Article 72 of the Constitution of India

Exercised on the mandatory aid and advice of the Union Council of Ministers (Article 74(1))
Subject to judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 (Maru Ram; Kehar Singh; Epuru Sudhakar; Shatrughan Chauhan)
essentialIngredients: Competent Authority: The President of India acting on the advice of the Union Cabinet / Ministry of Home Affairs.

Three Jurisdictional Gateways: (a) Cases where punishment or sentence is by a Court-martial (exclusive to President); (b) Cases where offence relates to a matter within Union executive power; (c) All cases where sentence is a sentence of death.

Five Modalities of Relief: (1) Pardon (completely absolves guilt and sentence, restoring citizen status); (2) Commutation (substitutes severe punishment with lighter form, e.g., death to life imprisonment); (3) Remission (reduces period of sentence without changing character, e.g., 10 years to 7 years rigorous imprisonment); (4) Respite (awards lesser sentence on special grounds, e.g., pregnancy or mental illness); (5) Reprieve (temporary stay of execution, especially death sentence, pending pardon petition).

Judicial Review Grounds (Epuru Sudhakar): Amenable to judicial review if: (a) Order passed without application of mind; (b) Order is mala fide; (c) Passed on wholly extraneous or irrelevant considerations; (d) Relevant materials kept out of consideration; (e) Order suffers from arbitrariness.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Article 72 represents the ultimate constitutional safety valve against judicial fallibility and excessive penal harshness.

### 1. Nature of the Power
In *Kehar Singh v. Union of India (1989)*, the Supreme Court clarified that the power under Article 72 is of the widest amplitude. It is not an appellate power over the courts; the President does not sit as a court of appeal. Rather, the President exercises an independent executive scrutiny to determine whether the convict merits mercy, and may scrutinize the evidence on record and come to a different conclusion from that arrived at by the judicial courts.

### 2. Aid and Advice of Council of Ministers
In *Maru Ram v. Union of India (1980)*, a Constitution Bench established that the President does NOT exercise clemency in personal discretion. The power under Article 72 is exercised strictly in accordance with the **aid and advice of the Central Government (Union Cabinet / Home Minister)** under Article 74(1).

### 3. Scope of Judicial Review
While the merits of the decision are not justiciable, the **manner of decision-making** is subject to judicial review:
- **Epuru Sudhakar v. Govt. of A.P. (2006):** The Supreme Court held that the clemency power is not beyond judicial scrutiny. If a pardon is granted on grounds of political affiliation, caste, or religious favoritism without considering the victims, it is arbitrary and void under Article 14.
- **Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India (2014):** A 3-judge bench held that inordinate, unexplained, and unreasonable executive delay in deciding mercy petitions of death-row convicts constitutes a violation of Article 21, and serves as a supervening ground for the Supreme Court to commute the death sentence to life imprisonment.
examples: Inordinate Delay in Deciding Death Mercy Petition: A convict sentenced to death files a mercy petition under Article 72 in 2012. The petition remains pending before the Ministry of Home Affairs without explanation for 11 years while the prisoner remains in solitary confinement. Applying Shatrughan Chauhan, the Supreme Court commutes the death sentence to life imprisonment for violation of Article 21 due to agonizing delay.

Arbitrary Clemency Based on Political Affiliation: A state governor under Article 161 (or President under Article 72) pardons a convicted politician belonging to the ruling party within 2 days of conviction without calling for prison reports or police records. Applying Epuru Sudhakar, the Supreme Court quashes the pardon for non-application of mind and political favoritism.
distinctions: Pardon vs Commutation: A pardon wipes out both the punishment and the guilt completely, restoring the convict to the status of an innocent person; commutation merely substitutes a harsher punishment with a milder one without removing the underlying criminal conviction.

Article 72 (President) vs Article 161 (Governor): The President alone has power over sentences awarded by Courts-martial; the President's death sentence clemency power is plenary across all laws, whereas a Governor's power under Article 161 covers state laws (though post-2021, Governors can commute death sentences in state law offences).
problemApplication: Issue: A mercy petition of a death-row convict is rejected by the President under Article 72. The convict's family discovers that the file submitted by the Ministry of Home Affairs mistakenly omitted the trial court's finding regarding the convict's juvenile age and severe mental illness. Can the rejection be challenged in the Supreme Court?
Rule: Under Epuru Sudhakar and Kehar Singh, judicial review lies where vital, relevant materials were kept out of consideration of the President, leading to non-application of mind.

Application: The omission of mental illness and juvenile status kept crucial mitigating factors away from the constitutional authority. The decision suffers from non-application of mind on vital records.
Counterargument: The Union argues that Article 72 is an unreviewable sovereign prerogative and court decrees cannot interfere with executive mercy.
Conclusion: The Supreme Court can set aside the rejection order and remand the matter to the President for fresh consideration with all relevant materials.
